claim.pdf_says:
a) If NUMERIC is specified,
1. If the category of the data item referenced by identifier-1 is numeric,
a. If the usage of the data item referenced by identifier-1 is implicitly or explicitly display or national, ...
b. If the usage of the data item referenced by identifier-1 is not display or national, ...
2. If the category of the data item referenced by identifier-1 is not numeric, ...
claim.markdown_says:
a) If NUMERIC is specified,

   1\. If the category of the data item referenced by identifier-1 is numeric,

   a. If the usage of the data item referenced by identifier-1 is implicitly or explicitly display or national, ...

   b. If the usage of the data item referenced by identifier-1 is not display or national, ...

   2\. If the category of the data item referenced by identifier-1 is not numeric, ...
claim.why_it_matters: In the PDF (8.8.4.1.3.3 GR2) items 1./2. are nested under a), and items a./b. are nested a further level under 1.; the markdown puts a), 1., a., b. and 2. all at one indentation, so the sub-items a./b. (usage display vs. not display) read as siblings of a) rather than as cases of 'category is numeric', and the a./b. labels collide with the a)/b) rule labels.

verdict.reasoning: Printed page 132 (PDF p154), 8.8.4.1.3.3 GR2: a) > 1. > a./b., then 2., indented in three levels. The markdown (page-154.md lines 41-49) has every item, word for word, in the same order and with the same labels: 'a)', '1.', 'a.', 'b.', '2.'. The only difference is that all five sit at one indentation. That is formatting. The labels keep the hierarchy readable: 'a)' (closing parenthesis) is the rule level, and 'a.'/'b.' (period) are the third level of the standard's own numbering scheme, so the labels do not collide. They sit between '1.' and '2.', which places them under 1. No text is missing, misplaced or misquoted, and the meaning does not change.
